---

## 2 Corinthians 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — “This is the third time I am coming to you. ‘Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.’”

**Traditional readings:**

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** Paul’s first visit founded the church (Acts 18:11) and lasted 18 months; the second was a brief, painful visit between the two Corinthian letters; now he prepares a third. Paul quotes Deuteronomy 19:15 to signal that this time he comes as a *judge*, not an investigator — there is already sufficient evidence to act decisively. [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill (Baptist):** Gill reckons the “three times” differently — one actual personal visit (Acts 18:1), a second “visit” by his first epistle (in which he spoke “as though present,” 1 Cor 5:3), and now a third by this second epistle. The quotation from Deuteronomy 19:15 is applied much as Christ applied it in Matthew 18:16: Paul proceeds judicially, and his repeated admonitions serve as the “witnesses” establishing the charges. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** He takes the “simple and natural meaning”: Paul will conduct a proper judicial inquiry on arrival, not act on rumours. Ellicott explicitly rejects the view that Paul personifies his visits as “three witnesses,” calling it “strained, almost fantastic” because it turns the judge into a prosecutor who appeals to his own repetition of charges as evidence. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Paul has “thrice formed the intention,” though the second time he had to forego his plan (2 Cor 1:15-17). The “two or three witnesses” probably represent Paul’s separate visits as separate attestations to the truths he preaches, rather than formal judicial proceedings. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 2 — “I already warned you the second time I was with you. So now in my absence I warn those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone.”

- **Guzik:** Paul has warned them before and now warns again. The situation required strong leadership; yet “rebellion against an appointed minister is rebellion against the higher power that appointed him” (Hughes). “I will not spare” are strong words, but the Corinthians’ immaturity called for them. [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** Paul had given a first admonition in his former epistle, and now a second before coming. This follows the pattern of Matthew 18 — first and second admonition, and if unsuccessful, he must proceed further. Paul says “if I come again” conditionally, submitting to God’s will about the journey. “I will not spare” means using his apostolic rod to punish incorrigible offenders, as he had done with the incestuous man, Hymenaeus and Philetus. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The earlier warning refers to 1 Cor 4:13-19 and the threat implied in 2 Cor 1:23. What Paul has in view is a sentence of excommunication — “delivering them to Satan” (1 Cor 5:5; 1 Tim 1:20) — with the confident expectation that the sentence would be followed by sharp bodily suffering. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “And to all other” means those who, though not fallen into gross sin, still rejected Paul’s authority and said he was afraid to come in person. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 3 — “since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.”

- **Guzik:** The Corinthian opponents (the “super-apostles” of 2 Cor 11:5 and 12:11) wanted to see more worldly “power” from Paul. Paul answers: “You want proof? When I come, you will see the power of God in my rebuke as I clean house. So clean it up before I come.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** The Corinthians called Paul’s apostleship into question and demanded proof — despite having been themselves the seals of his apostleship, and despite signs and wonders done among them, including the delivery of the incestuous person to Satan and the many struck with sickness and death (1 Cor 5:4; 11:30). This was not so much tempting Paul as tempting Christ in him. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** There is a “touch of indignant sadness” in Paul’s tone. Men will not be able to cast that reproach of weakness upon Christ “whose might they will feel all too keenly.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “Of the Christ who speaketh in me… but is mighty in you.” The Spirit of Christ, in spite of all their shortcomings, had not deserted them (see 1 Cor 1:6-7; 2:4). [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 4 — “For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power. And though we are weak in Him, yet by God’s power we will live with Him to serve you.”

- **Guzik:** Just as Jesus displayed weakness in crucifixion yet now reigns in resurrection power, so Paul will come with similar power after the Corinthians have seen his weakness. Harris notes: “in their immaturity the Corinthians were unimpressed by Christlike gentleness and meekness… but were overawed by arbitrary displays of power.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** Christ’s human nature was subject to all sinless infirmities — mortal, passible, liable to death — yet He was raised by divine power and now lives at God’s right hand vested with all power. The Corinthian Christians, encouraged by false apostles, despised Paul for his outward weakness. Paul sets Christ’s own pattern before them: as with the Head, so with His ministers. They are weak “in Him” (or “with Him,” as the Alexandrian copy and Syriac read), yet will live with Him by God’s power “toward you” — exercised in rebuking, admonishing, and using the apostolic rod. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The better manuscripts omit “though,” reading simply: “For even He was crucified out of weakness.” Christ is the highest representative of the law Paul himself had been comforted by — that strength is perfected in infirmity. The disciples share at once in their Lord’s weakness and His strength. The “life” here is not the future resurrection (though true in itself) but “the activities of the spiritual life… manifested in the exercise of spiritual power towards you and for your good.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “Out of weakness” — the human weakness Christ took upon Himself, which rendered Him liable to agony and death (Phil 2:7-8; Heb 2:10-18). The words “toward you” show that “the life of which he is thinking is the vigorous reestablishment of his spiritual authority in Christ over the Church of Corinth.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 5 — “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Can’t you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you — unless you actually fail the test?”

**This is the most debated verse in the chapter.** The traditional commentators and various Protestant traditions read it differently.

**Traditional readings:**

- **Guzik:** Paul asks a sobering question: “Am I really a Christian?” We are often ready to test others but must test ourselves first. “That was the trouble at Corinth. They criticized Paul and failed to examine themselves” (Redpath). Self-examination means submitting to the scrutiny of Christ Himself, asking Him to reveal what grieves His Spirit. The word for “disqualified” (*adokimos*) is the negative of “test” (*dokimazo*) — if we don’t test ourselves now, we may ultimately find we don’t pass. Guzik also quotes Spurgeon at length: “Do not merely sit in your closet and look at yourselves alone, but go out into this busy world and see what kind of piety you have. Remember, many a man’s religion will stand examination that will not stand proof.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** Paul directs the Corinthians to self-examination as a proof of Christ speaking in him: if they find themselves in the faith and Christ in them — blessings they received through Paul’s ministry — then they have their proof. “Except ye be reprobates” does not mean reprobate in the Calvinistic sense (standing opposed to the elect). Gill means those who lack judgment in spiritual things — like “reprobate silver,” counterfeit coin, disapproved. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The word “yourselves” is emphatically placed first in the Greek: “You seek a test of my power. Apply a test to yourselves.” “Examine” suggests a special test; “prove” suggests a general scrutiny. *Adokimos* means “failing to pass the scrutiny” — “Christ is in you… unless the sentence, after an impartial scrutiny, is that there are no tokens of His presence.” Ellicott explicitly says: “The ideas which Calvinistic theology has attached to the word ‘reprobate’ are… foreign to the true meaning of the word, both here and elsewhere.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “Prove your own selves” means “test your own sincerity.” *Adokimoi* means “tried and found to be worthless” — like “reprobate silver” in Jeremiah 6:30. The Pulpit Commentary echoes Ellicott: “The reader must not read Calvinistic horrors into an expression which gives no sanction to them.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

**Where Protestant traditions differ:**

- **Reformed view (MacArthur, Buswell):** Some in the Corinthian church were not genuine believers, and Paul challenges them to test whether they had ever truly been born again. Professing Christians should examine themselves for evidence of genuine conversion. MacArthur writes: “Doubts about one’s salvation are not wrong so long as they are not nursed… Scripture encourages self-examination.” This view treats the verse as addressing *justification* — are you truly saved? [(preceptaustin.org, from search excerpt)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-13-commentary)

- **Second view (sanctification):** Paul was not doubting the Corinthians’ salvation but calling them to examine the *quality of their walk with Christ* — ongoing sanctification, not once-for-all justification. Colin Kruse: Paul “wants them to see whether they are holding to the faith, i.e. the gospel, and conforming their lives to it.” The presence of Christ by the Spirit carries moral implications. [(preceptaustin.org, from search excerpt)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-13-commentary)

- **S. Lewis Johnson / “Hybrid” view (Dallas Theological Seminary):** Both objective assurance (looking to Scripture’s promises) and subjective assurance (examining one’s life for evidence) are valid. “True believers will see the glory of Christ reflected in their lives when they examine the genuineness of their salvation.” The Holy Spirit “bears witness with our spirit” (Rom 8:16) through both grounds. [(preceptaustin.org, from search excerpt)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-13-commentary)

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** In a lengthy sermon on this verse, Spurgeon distinguishes between being *in* the faith versus merely holding orthodox opinions *about* the faith. “There is the ark; and a number of men around it… ‘I believe that ark will swim’… Ay, but when the rain descended… it was not believing the ark as a matter of fact — it was *being in* the ark that saved men.” He also distinguishes “examine” (like a schoolmaster testing a student) from “prove” (like testing a horse before buying it — putting it through real-world trial). “Christ on Calvary will save no man, unless Christ be in the heart.” [(studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe)](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-corinthians-13.html)

> **Note on missing traditions:** Due to search limits, full pages from Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Methodist sources could not be fetched. From what was visible in the Precept Austin excerpts, the Reformed vs. sanctification-view debate dominates Protestant discussion of this verse, with the older Anglican commentators (Ellicott, Pulpit) pointedly rejecting a Calvinistic reading of *adokimos*.

---

### v. 6 — “And I hope you will realize that we have not failed the test.”

- **Guzik:** Paul anticipates the counter-question: “Well, why don’t you examine yourself, Paul?” He dismisses this: it is so apparent he is not disqualified that he simply trusts they recognize it. Yet he admits “though we may seem to be disqualified” if judged by worldly standards of power and success. [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** Whether the Corinthians were reprobate or not, Paul would not say — that he left to themselves. But he was confident he and his fellow apostles would give proof they were “not reprobates” — men of judgment in the Gospel, useful in ministry, approved by God. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** “Whether you fail to pass the test or not, I have a good hope that you will know that *we* do not fail, whether the test be that which you demand (v. 3), or that which I apply to myself as in the sight of God.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 7 — “Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong — not that we will appear to have stood the test, but that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed.”

- **Guzik:** Paul’s concern is for them, not his own reputation. He would rather appear weak and disqualified than have them sin and require his apostolic rod, which would prove his authority. [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** This shows Paul sought their good, not his own credit. If they sinned, his faithfulness in rebuking would be seen and his apostolic authority manifest in punishment — but he did not desire this. He “chose rather to be looked upon as a poor, mean, and insignificant person, than that they should sin.” This also demonstrates “the impotence of man’s free will, the necessity of the grace of God to abstain from sin, and perform good works.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** There is “a subtle play of thought and feeling.” He prays they be kept from evil and advance to positive holiness — “even though the result of that may be that we no longer put our apostolic supernatural powers into play, and so seem to fail in the trial to which you challenge us.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** This is “one of the intense expressions which, like Romans 9:3, spring from the earnest and passionate unselfishness of St. Paul.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 8 — “For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.”

- **Guzik:** Even the apostles were not above the truth. Paul could only work effectively *for* the truth, not against it. Hodge adds: “This passage is of special interest as fixing the limits of all ecclesiastical power… The promise of our Lord, that what the church binds on earth shall be bound in heaven, is limited by the condition that her decisions be in accordance with the truth.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** Apostles had no power against those who received, walked in, and held fast the truth of the Gospel. Their authority was “for the truth” — defending it by chastising those who contradicted or caused it to be blasphemed. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The deeper meaning: “We are content to seem to fail… for the condition of that [apostolic] power is that it is never exercised against the truth, and therefore if you walk in the truth, there will be no opening for its exercise.” The feeling is analogous to Romans 9:3 (“I could wish myself accursed”) and John 3:30 (“He must increase, but I must decrease”). [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “I am powerless against anything which is true, real, sincere; I can exercise no power except in the cause of the truth. Be true to the gospel, and you will be mighty and I shall be powerless, and… I shall rejoice at the result.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 9 — “In fact, we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong, and our prayer is for your perfection.”

- **Guzik:** If Paul’s weakness contributed to the Corinthians’ strength, he would be glad. His real concern was that they be “made complete.” They were strong in gifts but incomplete — “like a building built tall and strong — for one and a half walls, with the other walls crumbling or barely started.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** The apostles rejoiced when they had no occasion to exercise their authority — when the Corinthians stood fast in faith and walked as became the Gospel. “Your perfection” (or “restoration”) uses a metaphor from setting dislocated bones: the Corinthian church was like a disjointed body, and Paul wished their divisions healed and each member in its proper place. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** “Your restoration” — this is the only NT occurrence of the noun *katartisis*, though the related verb appears in “mending their nets” (Matt 4:21) and “restore” (Gal 6:1). Its proper meaning is “to bring back to completeness.” Paul’s seeming harshness and self-assertion, like his tenderness, were all aimed at restoring their first love and purity. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “Your perfection” means “your perfect union” — “the readjustment of your disordered elements.” Used in the Gospels for mending nets (Mark 1:19). [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 10 — “This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down.”

- **Guzik:** Paul preferred that the Corinthians clean up before he arrived. He wanted to use his authority for edification, not destruction. [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** Paul wrote to bring them to repentance so he would not need to use severity — such as striking people dead (as Peter did with Ananias and Sapphira) or delivering them to Satan. His authority was “to edification, and not to destruction.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The words “speak of an inner conflict, in which love has triumphed, not without pain, over feelings of bitterness and indignation. The storm has passed, and the sky is again clear. He does not recall what he has written, but he explains and half-apologises for it. It was better to speak with severity than to act.” Even had action been necessary, his aim would have been restoration, not punishment for its own sake or display of power. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The word “sharpness” (*apotomia*) is an adverb meaning “abruptly” or “precipitately” — the only other NT use is Titus 1:13, though the noun form appears in Romans 11:22 for “severity.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 11 — “Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you.”

- **Guzik:** “Farewell” is much better translated “rejoice” (*chairete*). Even after all the severity, Paul’s goal was that they would enjoy the joy of walking rightly with God. “Become complete” picks up the prayer of v. 9. Paul also proves that comfort, one-mindedness, and peace are at least partly in *our* power — we often wrongly assume they depend entirely on others. “It costs something… but the reward is worth it: the God of love and peace will be with you.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Wayne Barber (from search excerpt, Precept Austin):** Barber emphasizes “rejoice” as a present-tense imperative — “keep on rejoicing” — and a command, not a suggestion. “Wake up in the morning and be intentional: I’m going to live rejoicing in the Lord today no matter what happens.” Rejoicing is the fruit of walking in loving obedience to Christ. From rejoicing flow the other four commands: being made complete (putting things in order), being comforted, being like-minded about God’s message of grace, and living in peace. “The only way that this will ever take place is if Christ is living His life through you.” [(preceptaustin.org, from search excerpt)](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-13-commentary-wayne-barber)

- **Ellicott:** “Rejoice” (*chairete*) was the natural close of a Greek letter — adequately rendered “farewell” only if we remember it was used in all the fullness of its meaning. “Be perfect” = “restore yourselves to completeness; amend yourselves.” “Be of good comfort” echoes the opening of the epistle where “comfort” (*paraklēsis*) is a keynote (occurring 28 times in 2 Corinthians). “Be of one mind” recalls Paul’s grief over the schisms of 1 Corinthians 1–3. If these conditions are fulfilled, “the God of love and peace would assuredly be with them, for peace rests ever upon the son of peace (Luke 10:6).” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The concluding words are “marked by great gentleness, as though to heal the effects of the sharp rebuke and irony to which he has been compelled to have recourse.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 12 — “Greet one another with a holy kiss.”

- **Guzik:** The cultural equivalent today is a handshake or warm hug. It was “holy” — nothing to do with romantic affection. It was rarely done on Good Friday in remembrance of Judas’ kiss. By 1250 in England, the Archbishop of York introduced a “peace-board” kissed by clergy then passed around the congregation. Hodge wisely relates it to modern culture: “It is not a command of perpetual obligation… Christians should express their mutual love in the way sanctioned by the age and community in which they live.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Ellicott:** The aorist tense indicates a single act — when the epistle was publicly read, the hearers were to embrace and kiss each other’s cheeks “in token that all offences were forgotten and forgiven.” Justin Martyr (Apol. i. 65) places it before the Eucharistic oblation in Eastern liturgies. In the Western Church it came after the consecration. When suppressed in the 13th century, it was replaced by the *osculatorium* — kissing a carved marble or ivory tablet passed among the congregation. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The aorist tense shows it refers to a single act — “in sign of perfect unity and mutual forgiveness” — the kiss of peace. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 13 — “All the saints send you greetings.”

- **Ellicott:** The “saints” were those in Philippi where Paul was writing. The phrase shows Paul informed the church of one locality when writing to another, “and so made them feel that they were all members of the great family of God.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “All the saints; namely, in Philippi or Macedonia.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

### v. 14 — “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.”

- **Guzik:** This is the only place in the New Testament where Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are mentioned together in this kind of blessing. Paul wanted the Corinthians “completely blessed by everything God is.” Hodge: “For a Christian is one who seeks and enjoys the grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost.” [(enduringword.com)](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-13/)

- **Gill:** The epistle concludes with “a wish of all the blessings of grace from all the three persons, Father, Son, and Spirit.” [(biblehub.com/commentaries/gill)](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Ellicott:** The order is significant: usually the Father precedes the Son (2 Cor 1:2; Rom 1:7; 1 Cor 1:3), but here the order is inverted, “as though in the Apostle’s thoughts there was no ‘difference or inequality’ between them.” The sequence follows Paul’s own experience: he had just heard Christ say “My grace is sufficient for thee” (2 Cor 12:9); that grace flows from the love of the Father; and the fellowship (*koinōnia*) of the Spirit is what translates grace and love from abstract ideas into living experience (Phil 2:1; Rom 5:5). This benediction was adopted from a very early period in the liturgies of Antioch, Caesarea, and Jerusalem, and entered the Book of Common Prayer in 1559. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_corinthians/13.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “This is the only place where the full apostolic benediction occurs, and is alone sufficient to prove the doctrine of the Trinity. St. Paul seems to feel that the fullest benediction is needed at the close of the severest letter.” The word “all” is introduced with “special tenderness and graciousness. Some have sinned before; some have not repented; yet he has for them all one prayer and one blessing and one seal of holy apostolic love.” The superscription (though of no authority) correctly states the letter was written at Philippi and conveyed by Titus and possibly Luke. [(biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit)](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/13.htm)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences

**On verse 5 (“examine yourselves”):**
- **Reformed (MacArthur, Buswell):** The verse calls professing believers to test whether they have ever truly been born again — addressing the possibility of false conversion. Self-examination targets *justification*.
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** Spurgeon emphasizes the distinction between being *in* the faith versus merely holding correct opinions *about* the faith — the test is whether Christ actually dwells within. Gill sees the primary purpose as proving that Paul’s ministry was genuine (since the Corinthians’ faith came through it).
- **Anglican (Ellicott, Pulpit):** Both explicitly reject reading “reprobate” (*adokimos*) in a Calvinistic sense of eternal decree. The word simply means failing a test or being found worthless — like “reprobate silver.” They stress the immediate context: the Corinthians were testing Paul, so he turns the tables and tells them to test themselves.
- **Sanctification view (Kruse, others):** Paul addresses the *quality* of their walk, not their once-for-all salvation — “whether they are holding to the faith… and conforming their lives to it.”
- **Hybrid view (S. Lewis Johnson):** Both objective assurance (Scripture’s promises) and subjective assurance (self-examination for evidence) are valid and complementary.

**On verse 11 (“rejoice”):**
- The charismatic/dispensational reading (Wayne Barber via Precept Austin) emphasizes “rejoice” as a present-imperative command flowing from obedient relationship with Christ, with the subsequent commands flowing naturally from it — a more experiential, Spirit-filled-life emphasis.
